title: Ashrei (Psalm 145)
hook: said three times a day; the Talmud praises whoever says it daily (Berakhot 4b)

segments.voice: Yesterday, clean hands: Psalm twenty-four's answer at the gate, what you do and what you mean. Today, a prayer said three times a day.

If you've ever been to a weekday service in a synagogue, you've heard it, maybe without knowing its name. A fast, murmured rush of Hebrew, everyone at their own speed, one of the most-said passages in all of Jewish prayer. Twice every morning, once every afternoon. Three times a day, for a lifetime, adds up to tens of thousands of times. It begins with the word Ashrei, and it hides a small mystery in its alphabet.
screen: `A FAST, MURMURED RUSH OF HEBREW.` → `THREE TIMES A DAY.` → `A MYSTERY IN THE ALPHABET.`

segments.voice: Ashrei means happy, or fortunate: happy are those who dwell in Your house. Two verses from other psalms lead in, then comes the heart of it, Psalm one hundred forty-five. It's an acrostic: each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, aleph, bet, gimmel, all the way through. The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, says that whoever recites it three times a day is assured a place in the world to come. Then it asks: why this psalm, of all psalms? Because it goes through the alphabet? Other psalms do that too. The answer: because it goes through the alphabet and it contains this verse: "Thou openest Thy hand, and satisfiest every living thing with favour." Every living thing. Not just people, not just the righteous. The whole world, fed from an open hand. Many people slow down at that verse and say it with special attention. Now the mystery. One letter is missing: there's no verse for nun. The Talmud notices, and gives an answer. Nun would bring to mind a verse from the prophet Amos about Israel fallen, so the psalm leaves it out. And with the very next letter, samekh, it says: "The LORD upholdeth all that fall." The fall isn't mentioned. The catch comes first. An alphabet with a gap in it, and a hand stretched out over the gap.
screen: `ASHREI: HAPPY ARE THEY.` · `AN ALPHABET PSALM.` · `THOU OPENEST THY HAND.` · `NO NUN: THE CATCH BEFORE THE FALL.` · then, large: `THOU OPENEST THY HAND.`

segments.voice: If you have Psalm one forty-five nearby, read it slowly, all the way through, and slow down at the open-hand verse. If not, rest your hands in your lap, palms up, and think of what has come to you through open hands today, food, a kind word, a roof, a breath; then think of someone who's fallen lately, and imagine holding them up. If you pray, you can say the open-hand verse.
Ashrei. Happy are they. Psalm one forty-five, said three times a day: an alphabet with one letter missing, and an open hand that feeds every living thing.
Your line: thou openest thy hand. Every living thing, fed from it. Day three hundred nineteen, complete.

screen: `DAY 319 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A PSALM FOR EACH DAY.`

howItsDone: Ashrei is said twice in the morning service and once at the start of the afternoon service; many people say the open-hand verse with special concentration, and some touch their tefillin as they say it.
